questions.prompt: Put these steps of Cascade's build sequence, per Lesson 5's dependency chain, in the correct order.
items: Configure Accounts and Contacts, including record types and page layout basics
Build Leads with a conversion mapping into Account, Contact, and Opportunity
Configure Opportunities with Cascade's five named stages and Products
Create the two custom objects: Installation Project and Service Contract
Implement the full security model for real: roles, profiles, and sharing rules
Build Flows, validation rules, and the approval process
Build reports and the executive dashboard
questions.explain: Lesson 5's dependency chain runs on three rules: objects before automation, the data model before security implementation, and a working org before sample data and reports. That puts Accounts/Contacts first, then Leads (which convert into them), then Opportunities (which Lead conversion creates), then the two custom objects (Installation Project looks up to Opportunity), then the security model (sharing rules reference those custom objects), then automation (which must respect the finished security model), and finally reports, which need everything above to already exist.

questions.prompt: Match each Cascade employee to their role, per Lesson 2.
right: Sales Development Representative (SDR) who qualifies inbound Leads
questions.explain: Monica Reyes is VP of Sales, overseeing both sales teams. Priya Nair is the Senior Account Executive who owns Cascade's large, multi-location Key Accounts. Jordan Kessler is the SDR who qualifies every inbound Lead before conversion. Marcus Webb leads Service & Installation, the team that executes on-site equipment installs.

questions.prompt: Lesson 3 designs Installation Project's and Service Contract's relationships to Account and Opportunity as Lookup relationships rather than Master-Detail. Why?
options: A Lookup relationship lets each record's sharing and existence stand independent of its parent, which the separate sharing rules designed in Lesson 4 for the Service & Installation and Customer Success teams depend on
Master-Detail relationships aren't supported on custom objects in Salesforce
A Lookup relationship is required whenever a custom object references a standard object like Account or Opportunity
Lookup relationships automatically roll up Annual Value and Install Status to the parent Opportunity, which Master-Detail cannot do
questions.explain: Master-Detail would force Installation Project's and Service Contract's sharing to follow their parent exactly, which conflicts with the Lesson 4 sharing rules that grant the Service & Installation and Customer Success teams their own, separate access. Lookup keeps each custom object's sharing and existence independent of its parent, which is exactly what those sharing rules need to work.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Cascade's security model design from Lesson 4.
options: Account, Contact, Opportunity, Lead, Installation Project, and Service Contract are all set to Private at the Organization-Wide Default level
Priya Nair's role reports directly to Monica Reyes instead of through Derek Oyelaran, because Key Accounts deals are considered more sensitive
Monica Reyes gets her executive visibility from a separate 'Executive' profile created just for her
The Service & Installation team's sharing rule exists because installers don't report into the sales role hierarchy but still need to see the Opportunity behind an Installation Project
Role hierarchy access rolls both up and down equally, so a manager's visibility is identical to a direct report's
questions.explain: Every object in the model is Private at OWD. Priya Nair reports directly to Monica Reyes specifically so the New Business manager doesn't see Key Accounts deals by default. The Service & Installation sharing rule closes exactly the gap of installers sitting outside the sales role hierarchy. Monica's executive visibility comes from sitting at the top of the role hierarchy, not from a dedicated profile — she uses the ordinary Sales Manager profile. Role hierarchy access rolls up to managers, never down to subordinates.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: configuration done with Salesforce's point-and-click tools, such as objects, Flow, and validation rules, rather than written code, is called a ________ build.
questions.explain: Lesson 1's key terms define a declarative build as configuration done with Salesforce's point-and-click tools — objects, Flow, validation rules — rather than code. This capstone is explicitly scoped as a fully declarative build, which Lesson 18 later confirms by listing no Apex triggers or Lightning Web Components among what was built.

questions.prompt: In Salesforce, what is the primary function of a Record Type, as Lesson 6 uses it for Cascade's six Account segments (Restaurant, Hotel & Hospitality, Healthcare & Institutional, Education, Catering, Dealer)?
options: It controls which picklist values and which page layout a record uses, based on a category
It controls which users can see a record, independent of sharing rules
It permanently restricts which fields can ever be created on an object
It determines a record's owner automatically based on the category selected
It is a plain reportable field with no effect on page layout or picklist values
It replaces the need for Field-Level Security on a profile
questions.explain: A Record Type controls which page layout and which picklist values a user sees for a given category of record — exactly what Lesson 6 uses to give Restaurant, Hotel & Hospitality, Healthcare & Institutional, Education, Catering, and Dealer Accounts each their own picklist values, and later, in Lesson 10, their own page layout.
questions.distractorExplain: Option E describes Business Segment, not Record Type — Lesson 6 draws exactly this distinction. Record Type controls layout and picklist values; Business Segment is the separate plain field Chapter 4's reports filter on without worrying about Record Type IDs. Mixing the two up is the exact confusion the lesson calls out.

questions.prompt: Lesson 6 gives Account both a Record Type (e.g., Restaurant, Hotel & Hospitality) and a separate Business Segment picklist field. Why keep both, instead of relying on Record Type alone?
options: Record Type controls page layout and picklist values, while Business Segment is a plain field Chapter 4's reports can filter on without dealing with Record Type IDs
Business Segment is required because Record Type cannot have more than four values
Record Type is only visible to System Administrators, so Business Segment exists for everyone else
Business Segment automatically overrides Record Type whenever the two disagree
questions.explain: Lesson 6 explains that Record Type and Business Segment look redundant but aren't: Record Type governs page layout and picklist values, while Business Segment is a plain field that's simpler to filter and report on in Report Builder, which is exactly why Chapter 4's reports filter by Business Segment rather than Record Type.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Cascade's Opportunity stage configuration from Lesson 8.
options: Closed Won and Closed Lost are both marked as Closed stages, which is what triggers the Installation Project automation built in Chapter 3
Needs Analysis has a higher probability than Equipment Proposal
Qualifying is in the Pipeline forecast category, while Equipment Proposal and Negotiation/Review are both Best Case
Loss Reason is required on every Opportunity, regardless of stage
An Opportunity needs Products attached through Opportunity Product line items for it to represent more than a single dollar amount
questions.explain: Marking Closed Won and Closed Lost as Closed stages is what triggers the Chapter 3 Installation Project automation. Qualifying sits in Pipeline (10%) while Equipment Proposal (50%) and Negotiation/Review (75%) both sit in Best Case — Needs Analysis (25%) is actually lower than Equipment Proposal, not higher. Loss Reason is only required when Stage is Closed Lost, enforced by a Chapter 3 validation rule, not on every Opportunity. Products attached via Opportunity Product line items are exactly what turns a deal into a real equipment package instead of a bare number.

questions.prompt: Match each term from Lessons 3 and 9 to what it actually is.
right: The navigation entry that makes a custom object browsable in the Salesforce app
A reference between two objects where the child can exist and be reassigned independently of the parent
A record-naming format that generates automatically, like INST-0001, instead of requiring a human-entered name
A tighter reference where the child's security and existence are tied to the parent
questions.explain: A Lookup relationship lets the child exist and be reassigned independently of its parent. Master-Detail ties the child's security and existence tightly to its parent. Auto Number generates a record name automatically, like INST-0001, instead of requiring a human-entered one. A Custom Tab is the navigation entry that makes a custom object browsable in the app.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of converting a qualified Lead, per Lesson 7's walkthrough, in the correct order.
items: Jordan Kessler qualifies the Lead's budget and timeline by phone or email
Salesforce checks whether the Company name matches an existing Account, to avoid creating a duplicate
Salesforce creates (or updates) the Account and Contact using the conversion field mapping
Salesforce creates a new Opportunity, defaulted to the Qualifying stage
Jordan reassigns ownership of the new Account, Contact, and Opportunity to the correct rep
questions.explain: Jordan first qualifies the Lead by phone or email. Clicking Convert then runs Salesforce's own sequence: check for an existing Account by Company name, create or update the Account and Contact per the field mapping, and create a new Opportunity defaulted to Qualifying. Only after all of that does Jordan reassign ownership to Tom Baptiste or Priya Nair depending on account size.

questions.prompt: What is the primary function of a Salesforce validation rule, as Lesson 13 uses it across Cascade's Opportunity, Installation Project, and Service Contract records?
options: It blocks a record from saving when a formula evaluates to true, enforcing a specific data-quality condition
It automatically creates a related record whenever a field changes
It controls which profiles can edit a given field
It routes a record to a named approver for sign-off before it can proceed
It schedules a batch process to run against existing records overnight
It restricts which Record Type a user can select when creating a new record
questions.explain: A validation rule's error condition is a formula: when it evaluates to true, the save is blocked and an error message shows. Lesson 13's four rules all work exactly this way — Loss Reason required on Closed Lost, Decision Maker confirmed before Negotiation/Review, Target Install Date not in the past, and Annual Value must be positive.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D describes an approval process, which Lesson 14 builds separately — routing a record to a named approver like Monica Reyes for sign-off. A validation rule never routes anything anywhere; it only blocks or allows a save based on its own formula, with no approver involved at all.

questions.prompt: Tom Baptiste tries to move an Opportunity to Negotiation/Review. Primary Contact is set to a real Contact, but that Contact's Decision Maker checkbox is unchecked. What happens when Tom saves, per this Rule 2 error condition?
options: The save is blocked — Primary_Contact__c isn't blank, but NOT(Primary_Contact__r.Decision_Maker__c) is true, so the inner OR is still true and the rule fires
The save succeeds, because Primary Contact is set and ISBLANK(Primary_Contact__c) is false
The save is blocked, but only because the Opportunity has no Primary Contact at all
The rule doesn't evaluate at all until the Opportunity reaches Closed Won
questions.explain: The rule fires when the stage condition AND the contact condition are both true. The stage condition is true (Negotiation/Review). The contact condition is an OR: it's true if Primary Contact is blank OR the linked Contact isn't flagged Decision Maker. Here Primary Contact isn't blank, but the Contact's Decision Maker box is unchecked, so NOT(Primary_Contact__r.Decision_Maker__c) is true — the OR is still true, the AND fires, and the save is blocked.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the two Flows built in Lesson 12.
options: The New Lead Auto-Assignment Flow is a record-triggered Flow that runs after a Lead is saved, with no entry condition, so every new Lead qualifies
The Log a Service Visit Flow is a Screen Flow launched manually, typically from a Quick Action on the Installation Project page layout
The New Lead Auto-Assignment Flow requires a user to manually launch it from the Lead record
The Screen Flow gives installers full edit access to the Opportunity and Account fields on Installation Project
The New Lead Auto-Assignment Flow both reassigns ownership to Jordan Kessler and creates a same-day follow-up Task
questions.explain: The New Lead Auto-Assignment Flow is record-triggered, runs after save with no entry condition, and performs two actions: reassigning OwnerId to Jordan Kessler and creating a follow-up Task due the next day — not something a user launches by hand. The Log a Service Visit Flow is a Screen Flow, launched manually via a Quick Action on Installation Project. Opportunity and Account stay read-only on that layout, consistent with the Service Profile's permissions from Lesson 11 — installers never get edit access to them through this Flow.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Salesforce generates a ________ suffix for a custom lookup or master-detail field's relationship name — for example Primary_Contact__r — which is what lets a validation rule's formula reach across to a field on the related record.
questions.explain: Lesson 13 names this directly: the __r suffix is the relationship name Salesforce generates for a custom lookup or master-detail field, and it's what lets a formula like Primary_Contact__r.Decision_Maker__c traverse from Opportunity across to a field on the related Contact record.

questions.prompt: Lesson 15 sets the Cascade Executive Dashboard's running user to Monica Reyes instead of "run as logged-in user." Why?
options: Private OWD plus the role hierarchy means Monica sees every record beneath her, so running the dashboard as her guarantees it always shows the complete picture regardless of who's viewing it
"Run as logged-in user" is not a valid option for a dashboard built from an Opportunities report
Monica Reyes is the only user in the org with API access to the Reports tab
Running as a named user makes the dashboard refresh automatically every hour, which "run as logged-in user" cannot do
questions.explain: Since every object is Private at OWD and the role hierarchy rolls visibility up to Monica, running the dashboard as her specifically — rather than as whoever happens to be viewing it — guarantees the dashboard always shows the full picture, regardless of which user opens it.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about loading Cascade's sample data in Lesson 16.
options: Accounts and Contacts load first, through the Data Import Wizard, because every other object's sample data needs Accounts to already exist to look up to
Opportunities, Installation Projects, and Service Contracts load through Data Loader, which handles custom objects and multiple related lookups per row
Loading Opportunities before their related Accounts exist causes the lookup to silently save as blank with no error
Using Data Loader's Upsert operation with an External ID avoids creating duplicate Accounts if the same CSV gets loaded twice
Realistic sample data for Cascade means names like "Test Account 1" are acceptable as long as the volume of records is large enough
questions.explain: Accounts and Contacts load first through the Import Wizard since everything else looks up to Accounts. Opportunities, Installation Projects, and Service Contracts load through Data Loader for bulk insert and multiple related lookups. Data Loader rejects a row outright when a lookup has nothing to resolve to — it does not silently save a blank lookup, which is exactly why load order matters. Upsert with an External ID is what prevents duplicate Accounts on a repeated load. "Test Account 1"-style naming is explicitly called out as bad sample data regardless of volume — it tells you nothing about whether the build actually works.

questions.prompt: Match each section of the Lesson 18 handoff document to what it actually contains.
right: An honest, explicit list of what the build deliberately doesn't cover, such as no Apex triggers or outside ERP integration
The object-relationship diagram plus a table of every custom field added across Chapters 2–3, with its purpose
The role hierarchy diagram, the five-profile table, OWD settings, and all three sharing rules with the gap each one closes
Every Flow, validation rule, and the approval process, each with what triggers it, what it does, and why it exists
questions.explain: The Data Model section carries the Lesson 3 diagram plus the full custom field table. The Security Model section carries the Lesson 11 role hierarchy, the five profiles, OWD, and the three sharing rules with each gap explained. The Automation Inventory documents every Flow, validation rule, and the approval process with its trigger, behavior, and reason for existing. Known Limitations & Next Steps honestly lists what the build deliberately left out.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Lesson 18 calls documentation written for whoever inherits the org next — a new hire, a consultant, or an interviewer — rather than for the person who built it, a ________ document.
questions.explain: Lesson 18 draws this distinction directly: the Lesson 1 checklist tracks whether the build is finished, while the handoff document is written for whoever inherits the org next, structured so a new administrator could pick it up without the original builder in the room.

questions.prompt: Put these objects in the order Lesson 16 loads Cascade's sample data, so every lookup field has something to resolve to.
questions.explain: Accounts load first since nothing else can look up to them yet. Contacts follow, matched to those Accounts. Opportunities load next, looking up to Account. Installation Projects load after that, looking up to both Opportunity and Account. Service Contracts load last, since they can look up to both Account and Installation Project. Loading out of order means a lookup has nothing to resolve to, and Data Loader rejects the row rather than leaving it blank.

questions.prompt: Lesson 17's Section 1 security tests include a "negative test" — Login As Tom Baptiste, attempt to open a Service Contract, expect it to be blocked. Why include a negative test at all, not just tests that confirm access works?
options: Confirming access is correctly blocked is just as important as confirming it's correctly visible — a security model that only ever grants access and never verifies a denial isn't actually trustworthy
Negative tests are only needed when a validation rule, not a sharing rule, is involved
Tom Baptiste's profile is misconfigured on purpose, so the negative test exists to catch that specific bug
Negative tests replace the need to test the Lesson 12 Flows separately
questions.explain: Lesson 17 pairs positive-access tests with at least one negative test specifically because confirming a block works correctly is as important as confirming visibility works correctly — both are part of what makes a security model genuinely trustworthy, not just a model that happens to work when everything goes right.
